item.title: The service behind the saving
item.description:
The service behind the saving

Switch the equipment off and the consumption chart looks wonderful. We have found a very effective way to save electricity, and a rather poor way to cool a building. The absurd case is easy to see. It becomes less obvious when the pump is still running, the saving is smaller and the part of the building losing service is far from the screen.

Working on energy products made me suspicious of a lower number offered without its surrounding work. What did the plant deliver before, and what does it deliver now? Once that question enters the comparison, a saving becomes a much more interesting engineering problem.

What did we keep cooling?

In cooling, the output is not simply that a machine is running. The spaces being served need an acceptable result under particular conditions, which means two readings cannot be compared fairly just because they have the same unit. If the load, weather, operating hours or service requirement differs, the comparison may contain more than the effect of the intervention. A department closing, a load being outsourced or equipment operating for fewer hours can all lower consumption without improving efficiency. These can be sensible decisions, but they answer a different question from doing the same work with less energy. A product that wants to advise people has to distinguish these mechanisms, or it learns to praise whatever makes the number smaller.

The pump borrows work from the rest of the plant

A cooling system makes the boundary problem concrete. Changing a pump changes flow, which can alter the work at the chiller and the service delivered elsewhere. A cooling tower can consume more while allowing another component to consume less. The intervention must therefore be understood across the coupled operation: looking only at the device adjusted can miss both a benefit elsewhere and a harm elsewhere. The measurement boundary follows the question we are asking, rather than the convenience of the available meter.

The physical dependencies also complicate aggregation. A main meter and its subloads are not independent quantities to add. Two interventions can affect the same consumption, even if they have different names and appear on different pages of a report. Deciding what can be counted together is part of determining which improvement the engineering is trying to produce, not an accounting detail left until afterwards.

The experiment that changes the next experiment

An attractive intervention deserves a trial because the coupled behaviour is part of what we need to learn. Closing a valve and changing a pump setting are not equivalent interventions, even if both appear to concern the same flow. A suspected bottleneck may not be the limiting one; a component may behave differently from its nominal curve; the operating team may identify a service constraint the analysis missed. Testing the first arrangement can reveal why a second experiment should include another part of the system.

The possibility of stopping gives the trial value. A change that looks promising at one load may be inappropriate at another. Discovering that condition can improve the next experiment or show that continuing the disruption is unjustified. This is one reason I value the connection between product work and field observation: the field helps determine what the design should become. Retaining what was tried, what was observed and what condition changed gives the next experiment something to work from, without turning every discarded intervention into either an embarrassment or a delivered result.

A few hours on the chart, a year in the spreadsheet

A short observation can support a comparison for the hours it covers. It does not become a year of performance because a spreadsheet multiplies it by operating hours. Someone deciding whether to invest still needs an estimate of future benefit, but that estimate depends on the assumed hours, load, tariff, maintenance and continuation of the service. Keeping the measured comparison recognisable within the forecast prevents its uncertainty from disappearing exactly when the claim becomes larger.

Before-and-after charts need the same attention to their conditions. If the meter, the baseline or the way readings were collected changed, that belongs in the interpretation; a persuasive line cannot isolate a cause that the comparison did not isolate. Making those conditions available is a product challenge too. An operator should be able to understand why a comparison is relevant without having to reconstruct the analysis behind it.

Who pays for the saving?

Energy services add another layer. A provider may invest in equipment and continuing operation in exchange for a share of savings. The customer may avoid capital expense while accepting a particular service relationship. Physical energy reduction, avoided maintenance expense and tariff-dependent monetary saving are not identical benefits: a lower bill can reflect a price change, and an efficient plant can still encounter a higher tariff. The arrangement therefore needs an agreed baseline and a way to handle changed loads and periods. Those agreements connect the physical benefit to its commercial value; calculating a saving does not by itself produce an accepted report, an invoice or a payment.

My work on product and technology supported that continuing operation, alongside the teams responsible for energy services and commercial delivery. Installation began a relationship with the plant: observations, changed conditions and the customer's experience continued to affect what counted as a useful result.

When the chart starts giving instructions

Once a metric is visible and rewarded, people have a reason to optimise it. That makes its definition part of the product's behaviour. A system that celebrates consumption alone can encourage service loss; one that celebrates the number of successful commands can discourage investigation into what those commands achieved. The measure affects the work, so keeping it connected to the service is part of the design rather than a qualification added to the report.

Energy work gave me a concrete way to see this relationship between a measurable input and a contextual output. I find it useful in software too, though the mechanisms differ: a faster response can leave more work unfinished, or a lower ticket count can result from customers giving up. Understanding the work behind the number is what makes the comparison useful. In the plant, that means knowing what service continued before deciding what the saving was worth.

item.title: A question we can work on together
item.description:
A question we can work on together

In community work, I keep returning to the distance between having an interesting conversation and finding something we can do together. One person wants to study learning, another is interested in a new architecture, a third wants to build something useful immediately. I recognise something of myself in each position. The interests may belong to the same broad field without yet belonging to the same piece of work.

I volunteer with and help lead UPAI, the Uttar Pradesh AI community. Lucknow AI Labs, or LAI, is its founding Lucknow chapter. That association has given this question a practical setting. Helping a community grow and developing my own architectural ideas can happen in the same conversation, but they ask different things of the people listening. Someone may want to learn, offer a few hours, challenge the idea or simply observe. I do not want my enthusiasm for an architecture to decide which of those contributions counts.

Learning with a real problem gave my teaching a useful centre. I want shared research to have something similarly tangible: a question, an experiment or a stubborn result around which different people can contribute. The attraction is not merely distributing my plan among volunteers. It is finding an observation none of us could obtain merely by exchanging explanations.

Making the question small changes who can contribute

Time, interest and experience need separate attention. A person can know the subject and have little time; another can be a beginner with the patience to prepare examples carefully. Organisation, teaching, design and documentation also help research continue. Asking everybody to contribute code narrows the community before the question has even been chosen. I would rather find a piece of work small enough to carry, and clear enough that someone else can rely on it.

Consider an imagined group interested in whether retrieved context helps a language model use unfamiliar domain terms. “Build a system that understands the domain” is a large ambition. It leaves nearly every important choice open. A smaller question might ask whether short definitions improve answers to a fixed set of questions when the model and prompt are held constant. The result would not settle domain understanding. It would give the group a particular effect to investigate.

That reduction changes the work. Someone can read the relevant literature and clarify what previous comparisons actually measured. Someone can construct a small, permitted set of examples. Another person can implement the baseline and treatment. A reviewer can inspect whether the answers were judged consistently and whether the definitions accidentally contained the answers. These roles connect through the question. They are not separate personal projects placed under a common name.

It also gives disagreement somewhere useful to land. A participant might object that the questions are too easy, or that the definitions contain cues unavailable in ordinary use. The objection can improve the sample or narrow the claim. With a very broad ambition, the same disagreement often becomes an argument about the eventual architecture, long before the group has an observation to organise it.

A small question is not automatically an insignificant one. It can expose a dependency the larger ambition concealed. If the model succeeds only when the answer is effectively supplied in the context, the group has learned something different from successful transfer to new cases. If a simple baseline works equally well, a proposed mechanism may not yet have a useful job. The scale is modest enough that the disagreement can become an experiment.

Contribution needs a place to meet another contribution

Giving each volunteer a task does not guarantee that their work will connect. The reader of a paper may extract a definition that the implementation never uses. The person creating examples may make assumptions the reviewer does not know. The person writing the script may change the input format and unintentionally change the experiment. Coordination depends on making those interfaces intelligible.

For the imagined comparison, that could mean agreeing on the question format, the source of the definitions and what an acceptable answer contains. Each contribution can then be inspected where it joins the next. A participant who cannot write the model code can still expose a bad comparison or an ambiguous example. The experiment becomes a shared object around which people can develop different abilities.

There is a practical limit to how many things a volunteer can carry reliably. Research needs reading, data work, review and communication as well as the visible implementation. Expanding the proposal consumes all of those capacities, often before it consumes additional compute. A plan that leaves every spare evening occupied has made itself fragile. A smaller, repeatable commitment lets others build on a contribution without requiring perpetual enthusiasm from the same person.

This is different from making the work easy. Research will still contain confusion and periods when the result is hard to interpret. The useful arrangement gives that difficulty continuity: someone can explain the current state, another can take a small piece and both can return to the same question. It makes room for an observer to begin contributing without pretending that joining the discussion assigns them responsibility for the whole undertaking.

The artifact lets somebody else become a critic

A result explained only by the person who ran it cannot yet support much shared learning. The next participant needs enough of the configuration, inputs, method and output to understand what happened and try to challenge it. The relevant account is more specific than “the new approach worked.” It identifies what was changed and what was observed under that change.

The NeurIPS paper checklist asks for claims that match the contribution, experimental details and a reasonable way to reproduce or verify the result. Those questions are valuable before a paper exists. For our small group, they reveal whether the record is carrying the experiment or merely reporting enthusiasm about it. They do not require every research problem to use an identical release package.

The inputs matter as much as the script. The Datasheets for Datasets proposal connects a dataset's motivation, composition, collection and intended uses. Even a small sample benefits from knowing why these examples were selected and what they omit. Otherwise a later contributor can reuse a convenient file while quietly changing the meaning of the comparison.

Making an artifact inspectable is also a way of distributing intellectual responsibility. A newcomer can rerun a baseline, find a parsing problem or propose a counterexample. Their contribution need not begin with accepting the group's explanation. That is one reason reproducibility is educational as well as technical: it gives another person a place to encounter the claim through their own work.

A shared inquiry can change direction without losing itself

My own architectural exploration has changed as I have gone further into its foundations. A shared inquiry needs room for its explanation to change too. A community can help an idea become better precisely because it is not my team executing my product roadmap. Participants need enough of the question to disagree with it, and a way to make that disagreement useful without committing themselves to everything I want to investigate.

Suppose the comparison reveals that the definitions help familiar question forms but not a different phrasing. The group could respond by enlarging the system immediately. It could also keep the finding visible and investigate the dependence. That second movement may require less machinery and teach more. A question narrowed enough to begin should remain open enough to change when the result resists it.

There are many useful outcomes short of a novel paper: a faithful reproduction, a discovered error, an explanation of a limitation or a reusable evaluation case. They should be named for what they contribute. The ambition to produce new research can continue without treating every intermediate artifact as a new scientific result.

Credit needs a similarly careful account. Formulating the question, designing examples, implementing a comparison and interpreting its result are real contributions that can be made by different people. A community should make them legible rather than let the most visible speaker become the owner of everybody's work. That attention helps a participant understand both what they have contributed and what they still depend on others to do.

The deepest promise of shared research, for me, is that people can become more capable through the inquiry itself. The question gives them a common difficulty. The artifacts let the difficulty survive a particular conversation. Other people's criticism changes what each participant can see. A community begins to have continuity when that movement can happen again, even with a different person carrying the next part.

item.title: Learning with a real problem
item.description:
Learning with a real problem

A tutorial usually knows where it is going. It has chosen the important details, prepared the inputs and arranged a route to completion. A real problem is less courteous. Someone needs something to work; the information is incomplete, the environment resists the example and the person asking for help may not yet know how to describe what is wrong. That difficulty creates a reason to understand, not merely a reason to finish the exercise.

JouleLabs began close to the work

I founded and ran JouleLabs while building the product-development team at Smart Joules. The question was how someone still learning could make a meaningful contribution to consequential work. A problem statement needed to explain why the work mattered, a mentor needed to continue beyond the initial explanation, and the student's project needed a route through review towards something another person could use. Learning, contribution and possible recruitment could reinforce one another because they met around that shared object. Without the continuity, the student could produce a deliverable and the organisation a certificate, while neither acquired much that changed the next piece of work.

We reached our first university memorandum of understanding in under two months from the idea. The programme eventually involved five universities and a cohort of sixty-five students, with more than forty moving into full-time employment. Those numbers describe the programme’s reach and the transition into work. The educational question was what made that transition possible: a problem worth entering, someone available to review it and a team with a use for the result.

What is the dashboard supposed to change?

“Build a dashboard” specifies a deliverable. “Help an operator recognise why this measurement cannot yet be trusted” gives the learner a problem to investigate. The second formulation opens questions about the measurement, the operator's task and the decision that follows. It also makes review possible in a more meaningful way: did the person using the result gain something that helps them act? A dashboard might be the answer, but it would now have a reason for its contents.

The problem still needs a boundary. A learner cannot be expected to reconstruct an entire industrial system before making a first contribution. A mentor can isolate a useful question, identify what is safe to examine and provide enough context to prevent the project from becoming arbitrary guesswork. Too much prescription reduces the work to following steps; too little support turns confusion into a test of whether the learner can survive it. The scaffolding earns its place by making the next act of understanding possible, then leaving room for the learner to make it.

After the first explanation

A real project brings interruptions. The learner finds a missing assumption, the source changes or a first attempt fails. A mentor helps distinguish a useful failure from a misunderstanding that should not consume another week. That means making the problem navigable: where to look, what to compare, how to express the unresolved question and when to ask for help. It takes actual time within the team's work, not just an initial promise that help will be available.

The organisation also needs a way to receive the contribution. If nobody can review or integrate it, the learner's effort ends in a demonstration that has no continuing home. Supporting the programme therefore means reserving capacity on both sides: time for the student to enter the work, and time for the team to examine and use what they bring to it.

Two hours a week is a real commitment

In my UPAI community participation, time and continuity have been recurring questions. People arrive with different interests, abilities and amounts of unpaid time. A beginner asking for a learning path and an experienced volunteer able to help for two hours a week need different ways into the work. Enthusiasm is valuable, but scheduling it as though it were a permanent team can turn a broad assignment into something nobody can sustain.

A small commitment that someone can finish and another person can rely on can create more continuity. It gives a mentor something concrete to review and a learner a way to experience their contribution becoming useful. Designing participation around the support and time that exist need not exclude those still learning. It can make it easier for them to become capable of work they could not have done alone.

A contribution that keeps travelling

JouleLabs later inspired Sustainability Mafia’s Climate Ninja programme; I did not run that later programme. The influence interests me because the idea can travel beyond its first institution: practitioner-led learning around live problems gives people a route into useful work. A later programme can develop that route in ways its original setting could not.

This nearer form also connects to the longer ambition in The discipline after unlearning. A learner needs more than access to explanations. They need an environment in which a question can become a capability, and a capability can become a contribution.

There is something lovely about a learner discovering that their work has become useful to somebody else. That encounter asks for more care than a certificate does: a problem they can enter, somebody who stays through the confusion and a team willing to receive the result. Participants will want different futures, and some projects will lead somewhere other than integration. The point is to give curiosity enough contact with the world that the person can find their next contribution.

item.title: The discipline after unlearning
item.description:
The discipline after unlearning

It all started with “time”.

I could learn the engineering language for measuring a passage of time without feeling that I had answered what time was. The distinction sounds abstract until it unsettles a familiar explanation: a clock tells us something important, but naming the instrument does not finish the question.

That curiosity led me through technical study, philosophy and traditions I had grown up around. It also made me suspicious of a particular kind of education: the kind that gives us answers so efficiently that we stop noticing which questions those answers leave open.

Reading what I was told not to read

I grew up in Lucknow in a Hindu Brahmin family, with roots in Almora. A custom kept the Katha Upanishad away from ordinary reading, associating it with death. Being the rebel and curious soul I was, I read it anyway. What I found was, in a way, a podcast: a young boy, Nachiketa, in conversation with Yama about death, desire, what endures and what deserves to be pursued. The text became something I could examine for myself, rather than something defined by the inherited restriction around it.

I also wrote about the Nirvana Shatkam and its movement through negation: not this, not that. Reading it as a hymn was one encounter; following its negations as an exercise was another. Take away the identification with a body, a thought, a role or a description. What remains? In my reading, its movement towards Shiva and the bliss of consciousness was a process to go through, rather than a conclusion to repeat. It asked me to notice how quickly I had attached an identity to each thing it was taking away.

Other readings, including the Saundarya Lahari and Vigyan Bhairav, opened further paths. Ancient podcasts and publications, if you will, encountered through dialogue, negation, description and practice. Kaal, MahaKaal and Kaali became part of that inquiry: what were these texts saying about time through those names and images? All because I had been trying to find out what time was.

I began to wonder whether a civilisation organised around these inquiries understood something we have become poor at recognising. I called ours a civilisation of electromagnetism, a species of Maxwell, and imagined those older worlds through legends whose meanings might have been lost in translation. That is an intuition inviting study, not a historical demonstration supplied by the resemblance. What I wanted to recover was a scholarly encounter with the texts: enough freedom to question a custom, and enough patience to discover that the passage was not saying what I expected.

Unlearning, for me, began less as a declaration against a tradition than as a refusal to let the inherited instruction be the last thing said about it.

The comfort of a new allegiance

Once an inherited belief becomes questionable, rebellion can feel like clarity. The emotional reward arrives before the harder work. I can stop trusting an institution and begin trusting whichever voice most strongly opposes it, or adopt an unfamiliar explanation because its novelty feels liberating. Replacing the vocabulary leaves the old habit intact if I still accept conclusions without examining how they were reached. A question opens possibilities; the first alternative deserves examination too.

When I ask what time is, there are several kinds of work available. I can study what established physical theories say, examine how duration is experienced, read a story in which time is imagined differently, or propose a model and ask what observation would distinguish it from another. These inquiries can illuminate one another without supplying interchangeable answers. A compelling experience does not establish a physical mechanism; an equation does not tell me everything about how time is lived. Understanding what each encounter offers makes their connection useful, rather than merely exciting.

Getting very good at the teacher's answer

Education often rewards what can be repeated: a teacher needs some way to judge whether a learner has acquired the material. Yet a person can learn the vocabulary of independent thinking while becoming very skilled at anticipating what the teacher wants to hear. The same difference appears in technical work when a completed tutorial leaves the next unfamiliar condition unnavigable. Acquiring the explanation has value; making it one's own asks for another kind of encounter with the subject.

I am interested in learning that makes the learner more capable of noticing: what is missing from the explanation, which assumption was invisible before, or what they need to observe, build or experience to understand the question better. The result does not have to be certainty. A more precise doubt can give the next act of learning a direction.

The school I was imagining

The question led me to imagine an institution: a place where curiosity could develop through examining one's conditioning, meeting unfamiliar ideas and building something from the encounter. Individual advice can encourage inquiry, but the setting has to make it possible. The institution would need to support a learner through both the inherited answer and the uncertainty that opens when they question it.

That is a much longer project than improving a course outline. A school carries incentives, selection, authority, habits of discussion and an account of what counts as success. It can praise curiosity while punishing the questions that disrupt its own image.

The same scholarly detachment matters in modern research. I see it in open-source systems that let someone else examine the work, and in high-quality peer review that tries to judge an argument without favouring its desired outcome. Chasing a journal’s impact factor can displace that purpose. So can p-hacking: choosing and reworking analyses until the data appear to deliver the statistical result one wanted. An institution cannot teach detachment convincingly while rewarding the appearance of a successful result over an honest inquiry. It has to leave room to question even the concepts on which its own standing rests.

The difficult design problem is how to make inquiry ordinary. Learners need enough structure to become capable, enough freedom to discover a question of their own and enough care that disagreement does not become humiliation. Teachers need room to say they do not know without making every claim equally valid.

I imagine building such a place on a horizon longer than my own lifetime. Centuries of work, perhaps, and no guarantee that those who start it will live to see what it becomes. Detachment from the outcome is therefore part of the institution's design, not merely advice to its students. What would let later people examine its assumptions, rather than preserve the founder's answers? A school devoted to inquiry would eventually have to welcome a question that unsettled its own account of what inquiry was for. Otherwise the next generation would inherit another instruction not to read.

Practical teaching has given the question a nearer form. A real problem, a continuing mentor and work that somebody can use can connect curiosity to consequence. They do not fulfil the entire institutional ambition, but they create a place to begin.

A question that changes what I build

Time led me towards traditions, models and the creative inquiry I now pursue in Sleepwalker. Product work led me towards learning and institutions. Each encounter gave the next question more substance: an unexplained experience could prompt study; an incomplete explanation could prompt a design; teaching could expose an assumption I had stopped noticing.

These encounters keep the world from feeling exhausted by the answers I already have. They give curiosity something to return to, study and build upon. Questioning an explanation opens a space; the patient work that follows lets something richer grow there without making it another allegiance.

item.title: A future that remembers
item.description:
A future that remembers

Imagine a room with a terminal, a lamp, books and a cup somebody has left beside their work. Beyond the window, an immense machine hangs in the distance. Nobody in the room treats it as a spectacle. The lamp still has to light the desk; the person still has a page to finish. I find this future more interesting than one in which every ordinary object has disappeared into an immaculate wall.

What draws me to it is the possibility of technological change without cultural amnesia. An inherited form need not be a relic, and an advanced instrument need not look as though it arrived from outside the life around it. A civilisation can maintain its objects, rituals and places while discovering new things they can do. The future I want to imagine has had time to become familiar.

A machine with a history

A perfectly seamless device invites me to treat it as a finished surface. A housing, a switch, an instrument panel or a visible connection gives it a body. Someone may have opened it, changed a part, understood its behaviour well enough to keep it running. Those possibilities alter the world implied by the image. The object belongs to a history of use rather than merely a catalogue of the latest technology.

That is part of my attraction to analog technological futures. Rounded screens, deep bezels, lamps and physical controls are forms I can imagine being inhabited, maintained and passed on. Their significance is not that old hardware was universally better. It is that technology occupies a place in human life. When everything becomes a frictionless pane, I can lose the sense of how a person relates to what sustains them.

The same thought changes how I imagine a sacred or civic building. A temple containing an advanced instrument need not be a temple with a futuristic accessory pasted onto it. What if its material, spatial customs, maintenance and observation had developed together? A shrine and a terminal room could come from the same technological tradition. I want to discover how that continuity would feel in a world, rather than make a historical claim by drawing the two beside each other.

Recognition, followed by surprise

There is a particular encounter I keep trying to design: an object first appears familiar, then turns out to be doing something I did not expect. At rest, it has the discipline of an artifact. In use, a held state, a movement or a change of light reveals that it is alive as a system. Recognition gives the surprise somewhere to land. Without it, the experience can become another sequence of impressive effects with nothing to hold onto.

That ambition was behind my earlier studies of programmable geometry, interfaces and expressive physical objects. I wanted an identity that could move between a screen, a light and a piece of sound without becoming a logo repeatedly applied to different surfaces. The more difficult question was when that range should appear. If everything moves, movement stops telling me anything. If the system is so restrained that it never reveals its character, the restraint has become a loss of possibility.

The dragon drainpipe is a useful image for what I mean. It carries water away and still has a face, a story, a little delight. Its poetry has not excused it from doing the ordinary job. Its ordinary job has not required it to abandon the poetry. I want technology to hold that conjunction more often: something exact enough to trust and alive enough to care about.

A quiet frame for a vivid world

The frame around an experience can demand attention that the experience needed for itself. A reader may arrive to follow an argument and spend their first moments learning a new navigation ritual. An image may be crowded by surrounding effects, each announcing that the interface is special. I want the machinery to spend that attention carefully. A clear, addressable interaction can remain quiet until it is called, then respond directly.

The terminal interests me in this sense: naming, querying, changing a state and seeing a response. I do not need a screen full of fake prompts to preserve that manner. In a publication, the reading surface can carry stable habits while the world around the work changes through material, geometry, type and light. The reader should not have to relearn how to move every time the atmosphere becomes different.

An image then has room to carry more of the expressive burden. A cool field and one warm source can establish a relation before detailed textures establish materials. Overlap, distance and a silhouette can make a place dimensional without making every surface equally explicit. This is why I care about the composition of a human witness within a larger world. What matters first is where the person stands in relation to the light, the opening, the thing that exceeds them. An inventory of beautiful surfaces can leave that relation strangely absent.

Ordinary life gives the immense world weight

A monumental image can make a person useful only as a ruler. A small figure demonstrates that the structure is large, then has no more work to do. I want the figure to carry something of a life. A desk, a return path, a recognisable object or a lit window can suggest that the place has uses beyond the moment we are watching. The extraordinary becomes more convincing when the world can afford to treat some of it as ordinary.

That conviction reaches into how I think about an actual working space. Books, music, research and making need room alongside the rest of a household's life. The design should absorb difficult services and connections so the room can remain open, usable and quiet. I do not want every technical possibility to become something its inhabitants must constantly operate. Nor do I want the quietness to depend on pretending the systems underneath it do not exist.

A future acquires depth when some things persist through its transformations. In a sequence, a remembered object or a stable threshold can carry that persistence even as the surrounding register changes. In a technological world, an inherited custom or repairable instrument can do similar imaginative work. It gives the new thing a relation to what was already there.

I want a future with enough memory that people can belong to it, and enough possibility that belonging does not become a demand to leave everything unchanged. The books and the terminal can share a desk. The enormous machine can remain outside the window while someone finishes a page. The future has happened, and life has continued within it.

item.title: A lifetime in the larger frame
item.description:
A lifetime in the larger frame

Imagine someone looking at an entire life and calling it a moment. Inside it, there were mornings that would not end, years that passed before anyone noticed, promises, work, boredom and people who mattered. From the larger frame, all of that fits into barely a pause. Have we discovered that the life was insignificant, or only that we were looking from far away?

The question returns whenever I place a familiar interval beside an unfamiliar scale. A breath has a beginning and an end I can attend to. A cosmic period can be written as a number so large that my attention has no sensible way to inhabit it. Repeating breaths gives me a ratio, then exhausts my imagination long before the arithmetic runs out. I am interested in the point where a perfectly intelligible calculation stops being a satisfactory encounter with what it describes.

What the larger frame leaves out

A year can contain an ordinary day that will later matter enormously. At the time, I may not know which day it is. A short conversation can change how I understand years of work; an afternoon can begin a question that keeps returning. Looking backwards makes a few moments appear inevitable because the rest has fallen out of the account. The life as experienced was less selective. It included the waiting, false starts and intervals whose significance was not yet visible.

That makes scale more than a matter of zoom. A career summary, a personal recollection and a calendar arrange the same duration around different questions. The summary selects contributions. The recollection follows what it felt like to become the person who made them. The calendar keeps a common measure through both. None needs to contain everything, but I lose something when I forget why a particular account was made and ask it to stand for the whole life.

Even a very ordinary wait makes the difference felt. Waiting for an important reply and becoming absorbed in a piece of work can occupy the same measured interval. The difference is not a defect in the clock. Attention is organised around a different possibility: in one interval I keep returning to what has not happened; in the other, the work keeps offering another relation to follow. Duration meets a person through what they are doing, expecting and unable to settle.

Recognition inside an impossible world

In the Markandeya account, the change of scale does not dissolve the familiar. In the Bhaktivedanta rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the witness enters the child's body and finds a world within it; 12.9.30 brings recognition as close as his own hermitage. The world becomes impossible around a place he knows. Its immensity reaches him through recognition.

Vastness can be represented by making a figure smaller and smaller until the figure hardly matters. Keeping enough of the figure's world offers another possibility: the change of frame becomes an encounter. A place, a remembered route or an ordinary object can carry a relation that sheer magnitude cannot. That is the attraction of the familiar surviving within Markandeya's immense frame. It lets recognition deepen the bewilderment instead of ending it.

For a drawing or an imagined scene, this suggests a question: which familiar detail should survive as the frame expands? A place the witness knows could hold more of the encounter than another dramatic display of magnitude. The intimate remains intimate after the frame expands, and its persistence changes how the expanded world feels.

The observer brings a small world

An observer never arrives empty. Even an instrument records particular quantities at a particular resolution; a person also brings memory, expectation and attachment. I can ask precisely how a record retained a distinction in the research on recoverable observations. Here I am asking what it means to carry a small world into a larger encounter. The fact that a description can omit that world does not make it disappear from the person undergoing the experience.

A cosmic perspective can be generous when it loosens an immediate problem's claim to be everything. It can also become a convenient way of dismissing the problem. A deadline is small against a century. Someone waiting on its result may still have a good reason to care. A disagreement can become less absolute when placed in a longer life without making every participant's cost imaginary. I want the wider frame to change my judgment, not excuse me from looking at what remains close.

This is why I keep returning to Breath of Cosmos. That argument takes an unbounded duration and a finite, seven-second breath: the count of human intervals grows without bound, while one interval's share tends to zero. The breath itself remains nonzero. Its smallness belongs to the comparison, which is precisely why I do not want the comparison to erase the experience. Sleepwalker's world inside a breath follows the image into a creative question: what can a witness recognise as the frame expands?

The larger view is not a place where I can finally put life down and describe it without involvement. I am still the person doing the looking. A lifetime may occupy a tiny fraction of the span I can imagine, yet that is the fraction through which I encounter the span at all. Calling it small has measured a relation. What it means to live it remains to be understood.

item.title: The intelligence between the parts
item.description:
The intelligence between the parts

Imagine finding a useful piece of intelligence and putting it beside another. One recognises a situation; the other knows what to do when that situation appears. Connecting them sounds almost embarrassingly straightforward. Recognition goes in, action comes out. But what exactly passed between them? A label, a history, a degree of uncertainty, the thing one of them noticed and the other would otherwise miss? The connection may be carrying more of the intelligence than the diagram admits.

This is a question I have been following through different kinds of work. At DAO Studio, the operating-system image helped me think about applications, agents and playbooks. A capability could have an interface; a sequence could retain what an earlier step had found; a later step could resume when the missing information arrived. Those were useful ways to arrange work. Underneath them was another ambition that arranging calls could not satisfy: could learned capacities themselves become composable, and could their organisation change what the whole system was able to do?

The missing part of the handoff

Suppose one component reads a passage and reports that a person promised to return. Another selects the next action. The report may be accurate and still be too small. Was the promise conditional? Did it concern tomorrow or a date that has already passed? Was it spoken sincerely, quoted from someone else or inferred by the reader? If the second component needs one of those distinctions, an impeccably delivered label cannot supply it. The apparent quality of the first component conceals an unanswered question about what the two can share.

An application can often solve this through an explicit representation. Carry the relevant fields, retain the source, let the next step ask for what it needs. The agent and playbook work gave that approach a concrete home. I still find it valuable: a visible sequence can expose the point at which interpretation, missing information or a person's decision matters. Yet the more interesting research possibility begins when I cannot specify the whole useful representation in advance. What would let two learned components discover a productive exchange rather than merely conform to the exchange I designed for them?

That question changes the object I am trying to build. A pipeline can work because its author anticipated the intermediate states. A population of learned units would have to make useful states available through its own limited interaction. It might discover a better division of labour, or spend all its time communicating. Giving each unit a name and drawing arrows between them tells me very little about which of those happened.

A capacity has a setting

The idea of reusable intelligence is attractive partly because software reuse makes it feel familiar. A library function can arrive with a declared input, output and contract. A learned capacity also arrives with a history: examples, surrounding representations, assumptions about the other parts and the resources under which it worked. I cannot treat that history as incidental packaging if changing it changes the capacity.

Consider moving a summariser from a short exchange to a long negotiation. It may still return a fluent account, but the important distinction might now be which proposals were accepted, which were withdrawn and which party could make them. “It summarises” is a poor description of what I need to reuse. A richer account asks what the capacity preserves, when it fails and which downstream decisions remain possible. This is the pressure behind keeping context inside a reusable capability: the useful unit is larger than the attractive output.

I work on the practical side of that question through Pale: make a person-described world operational, with relationships and capabilities the system can already inspect. Counsel supplies local semantic judgment inside that arrangement. The deeper architectural question is how much of the useful organisation could itself be learned, instead of requiring me to specify every exchange.

My research in Causality separates the question of one unit from the question of many. MUON asks what a small adaptive unit might be; HENA asks what organisation among units might make possible. The relationship between Counsel and MUON, and between Pale and HENA, gives me two scales at which to follow the ambition. A better unit could change the judgment within an arrangement; a better many-unit architecture could change how the arrangement itself reasons and organises. The surrounding experience could become simpler as the intelligence beneath it learns more of that work. That separation gives the ambition something to work against. If I change a unit and the whole improves, did the unit improve, did its communication become easier, or did the arrangement give it more resources? I want to understand the contribution, because the answer determines what is reusable.

There are narrower ways into the compatibility question. Git Re-Basin studies aligning hidden units through permutations before merging independently trained models in weight space. It gives me something more precise than the wish to move a useful piece of intelligence: what transformation would make two representations compatible, and what behaviour should survive the combination? That is not yet the same as locating a separable capacity to transfer, but it makes one part of the difficulty available for investigation.

Memory makes the arrangement matter

Imagine a clue arriving early, before anyone knows why it is important. Much later, another part receives a request for which that clue would be decisive. The first part can keep the clue, but keeping it privately does not help the second. Broadcasting everything would make it available and defeat the point of a limited system. A useful arrangement has to make some combination of retention, routing and later recognition work together.

This is why distributed memory interests me more than a large bag of messages. The arrangement decides what can become relevant across time. A small unit may have enough capability for its local task while the population fails because nobody can find what another unit kept. Conversely, a simple unit can become useful through a well-placed connection. The early-clue construction makes that problem small enough to examine: local competence and collective usefulness are different things we can actually compare.

There is a personal attraction here too. I work across fields in which something encountered casually can become useful much later. The temptation is to call that cross-pollination and leave its operation mysterious. Research lets me ask a narrower question without losing the attraction: what survived the interval, what made it accessible and what did the later work gain from it? A system that simply repeats more of its past has not necessarily become more capable of making those connections.

The operating-system image remains useful to me, but it now opens onto several different problems. There is the arrangement of work that I can describe explicitly. There is the learned capacity that I would like to understand well enough to move. There is the organisation that might make partial capacities useful together. I do not need one familiar metaphor to finish all three. What keeps me following them is the possibility that intelligence can live partly in how an encounter is carried forward, not only in the component that first understood it.

item.title: Thinking in more than one medium
item.description:
Thinking in more than one medium

Draw a person beside a doorway. Then draw the doorway so large that the person nearly disappears. The objects are the same; the encounter is not. Put a light inside the opening and the person's relation to it changes again. I can describe those changes in words, but making the image gives them a form my explanation might never have asked for.

That is why creative work matters to my thinking beyond its eventual artifact. An image, a piece of sound or a sequence is not merely a delivery format for an idea already finished elsewhere. The form can make something available to attention that I had not yet understood. I want room to discover that difference before deciding whether it belongs in a story, a design, an argument or a more precise investigation.

Writing has mattered to me in a more personal way, too. Taking it seriously helped me with anxiety. An upsetting experience can consume attention, but it can also become a prompt for creative work. My instinct has been to observe and move on, spending that attention where something can grow, personally or professionally. Writing can be an outlet for that movement.

The diagram asks for a relation

A diagram is often useful because it refuses some of the richness of the situation. Give it events and arrows, and I have to decide what an arrow means. Dependence? Order? A message? A person's inference? When I cannot answer, the drawing has exposed something that an expansive paragraph could keep pleasantly vague. The small representation has made a particular question unavoidable.

Yet the diagram can also become too persuasive. A line drawn between two things makes the connection look settled. Equal circles make different objects appear interchangeable. Putting one box above another suggests a hierarchy that might belong only to the page. I try to keep the act of drawing available to revision: erase an arrow, change a boundary, ask which relation disappeared. In the inquiry into changing descriptions, that difficulty becomes explicit. A language can answer everything it knows how to ask and still leave the needed relation outside it.

Creative work lets me encounter a related difficulty from another direction. What if the relation is visible in an image but has not yet become a clear statement? An illustrated threshold might give me hesitation, invitation or dread before I can say exactly which arrangement produced it. I can develop the composition while trying to understand the effect. Naming it too early may narrow the work to an interpretation the image had already exceeded.

Sound gives a thought an interval

A static mark can be encountered almost at once. Sound asks for an interval. A returning tone, a sustained note or a silence has a relation to what came before and to what I expect next. Consider an imagined instrument that changes its sound when it enters a held state. If every movement produces another alert, I may stop hearing the state and start hearing the interruptions. If the change is too subtle, the relation may never become available at all. The expressive problem is also a problem of attention.

My earlier creator studies explored that relation through programmable geometry, music visualisers, lighting and an expressive lamp. These were ways of asking how one form could become active across different media. A shape could move with sound; an object could reveal its orientation; a light could hold a quiet state. The attraction was not simply to synchronise effects. It was to discover which transformations kept a recognisable character while making the present encounter meaningful.

Music remains part of my personal creative practice, alongside drawing and technical work. I do not need to make each practice justify itself as a product. Nor do I want to flatten them into one universal method: a sound's temporal relation and a picture's spatial relation give me different things to work with. Their exchange becomes useful when I can hear or see the difference, rather than declare in advance that everything is geometry.

A sequence gives the reader some of the work

Now put the person outside the doorway in one frame and inside in the next. Something happened in the interval nobody drew. The reader supplies it. Change the second frame, delay it or place it after a turn of the page, and the supplied relation changes. I find that participation more interesting than a sequence of increasingly spectacular images. The page can make the reader discover something instead of announcing how it should feel.

This is one of the reasons the space between panels matters to the work I am developing in Sleepwalker. The image has a place within an order of attention. A beautiful frame can become the wrong frame if it reveals what the sequence needs to withhold. A quiet detail can become decisive when the reader returns to it with another understanding. The work is partly in the relation the page leaves open.

A narrative has more than one arrangement to hold. An event happened; somebody understood it incorrectly; a reader encountered that account before encountering the event. Revising the reader's discovery need not revise what happened. I am drawn to these several orders of a story because they let an idea retain its consequences while changing how it is encountered. The model gives the author more room to compose. It does not choose what the composition should mean.

Let the crossing change something

A mathematical question can make me notice a visual relation. A traditional passage can give an imagined scene a difficulty to hold. An image can make me ask why a person still matters in an enormous frame. Those crossings are part of one person's inquiry without making all the forms interchangeable. A scene can be exact about what a witness encounters while leaving its world physically impossible. A formal construction can be exact about a small question while leaving most of the witness's life outside it.

I used to reach for large pictures because they gave an unfamiliar thought somewhere to begin. I still want that reach. What changes as the work develops is the willingness to let a form answer back: a calculation exposes the false step, a scene asks for the omitted person, a sequence reveals that the order made the meaning. Each can send me back to the question with something I did not bring into the first attempt.

Keeping those practices alive together is different from deciding that every drawing is research or every curiosity needs a public project. Some work should remain play. Some questions need the patience of study. Some acquire a useful technical form; others become more honest through an image. I want a working life in which I can follow those changes without asking one title to explain them all.

The artifact is where somebody else may eventually meet the inquiry. Before that, making it is already a way of thinking. The doorway can remain a doorway while becoming something I did not know I was trying to understand.

item.title: What I want a memory to do
item.description:
What I want a memory to do

Suppose I write something down because I cannot yet understand why it interests me. Months later, another question arrives and the earlier thought becomes useful. The note did not improve while it waited. Something changed in the relation between what I had kept and what I was trying to understand. That is the part of memory I find most difficult to design for: I would like to preserve the possibility without preserving everything as though everything were equally important.

It is easy to confuse the size of an archive with the reach of a mind. More material can give a question more to meet. It can also give an old explanation more ways to keep returning. A memory that retrieves the same persuasive account whenever I encounter difficulty may help me continue, or prevent me from noticing that the difficulty has changed. What I want from it is closer to a productive encounter than to a reliable repetition.

A note waiting for its question

Imagine keeping a description of how two pieces of equipment connect. For months, the description is less useful than an ordinary stock count. Then a repair fails because the available replacement does not fit. The old connection detail becomes decisive. The memory did not need to predict the exact repair in order to retain something valuable, but the retained detail still needs a route into the new question. An archive can contain it and leave the person asking about it none the wiser.

My interest in this goes beyond searching by a better phrase. A new question may reorganise what the old material means. The word “available” might once have meant “present in the store”; it now has to mean “usable for this machine”. The stock-and-compatibility construction makes that change visible. If my account has no place for compatibility, a more confident answer about stock does not help. I need to revisit the description, not just retrieve a better value within it.

This is also what makes rereading worthwhile. I can return to the same passage with a question I did not have before and notice a relation that familiarity concealed. The words remain, yet the encounter changes. A note is most valuable to me when it can reconnect me with that possibility: enough of the source, enough of the question I was following, enough of what I had not settled. A conclusion detached from all three can be memorably phrased and remarkably hard to use.

Three different ways to change

When an experience does not fit my expectation, several responses are possible. I can keep the exception alongside the account. I can adjust the account. Or I can discover that its categories were too small for the question. Those responses operate at different depths. Treating every exception as a reason to rebuild everything makes learning unstable; treating every exception as another item to file makes the original explanation almost impossible to disturb.

The distinction has become a research question for me. In MUON's surprise inquiry, retaining something, changing a learned parameter and proposing a structural change are separate responses. I am interested in the choice between them. A discrepancy is valuable because it creates work for the explanation, not because its intensity tells us which explanation should replace it. The inconvenient observation may be a mistake, a rare event, a changed situation or the missing distinction that makes the rest intelligible.

That keeps the ambition alive without making the machinery a portrait of a person. A learning experiment can define precisely what a retained cue, an update or a change of structure means in its small world. My own experience is messier: I do not have a loss function for everything I care about, and usefulness can change because my commitments changed. The experiment gives one part of the difficulty a form I can examine. It does not need to explain the whole of learning to be worth doing.

Useful after the moment has passed

A cue can matter long after the response that preserved it. Suppose a system sees a signal early, receives an unrelated stream, and is asked much later to act on that signal. A method that excels at the intervening work can still fail because it discarded the one earlier distinction the later task needed. I find this a more revealing memory problem than asking whether a stored phrase can be repeated immediately. The interval gives retention a consequence.

Reckon gives that interest a laboratory setting: retained records and their use can be varied within its benchmark tasks. The related question of updating after feedback asks how a later outcome should change an earlier estimate. An old success need not outweigh a changed situation indefinitely; a recent failure need not erase everything before it. The shape of the update expresses what we think the history still tells us.

Outside the laboratory, I often want to keep an unfinished thought because it may meet another field later. That possibility is a reason to retain its distinctive question, not to call every collected fragment important. A future connection needs something specific to connect with. When I compress a thought to “interesting idea about learning”, I have preserved my enthusiasm and discarded most of what another inquiry could use.

What difference did remembering make?

Finding the note feels like success because something familiar returned. The more interesting question is what I could do after finding it. Did it expose the assumption I had forgotten? Did it change a decision? Did it save me from repeating a failed approach, or simply lend another quotation to the approach I already favoured? An opened document is a weak answer to those questions.

Scope brings that question into the working environment I am building. I want it to remember more than relevant passages: the people around a task, the long game of a project and the context that makes the same words mean something different in another relationship. The descriptive picture should help an agent meet the situation without making it a permanent judgment about the people in it.

This is the pressure behind learning which context actually helps. Frequency can tell a system what I tend to retrieve; it cannot by itself tell the system whether my habit was useful. Something rarely used can be indispensable when its particular condition appears. Something frequently opened can have become a comfortable distraction. I want a memory that becomes sensitive to that difference, rather than one that makes my previous preferences harder to escape.

The technical ambition brings me back to an ordinary personal difficulty. A thought can survive as a sentence and lose the question that made it alive. It can return so familiarly that I mistake recognition for help. I do not want every unfinished thought to become a lifelong obligation. I want the ones that survive to carry enough of their encounter that, when another question arrives, they offer more than the fact that I once found them interesting.
